one_liner: Fails the quality test (weak financial health), so price does not matter.

profile.what: Wells Fargo is a large US consumer and commercial bank, with the biggest branch network in the country, mortgage and auto lending, cards and a wealth-management business.
profile.money: Mostly net interest income from loans funded by deposits, plus fees from wealth management, cards and banking. In 2025 the Federal Reserve lifted the cap on its asset size imposed after its fake-accounts scandal, freeing it to grow its balance sheet again.
profile.valued: Valued on price to tangible book and P/E. The multiple has risen with the removal of the asset cap and depends on reaching its target return on tangible equity.
profile.peer_group: Financials · bank, insurer or asset manager

summary.sentence: A large bank free to grow again after years under a regulatory cap.
risks: Revenue has not grown in five years.

meaning.what_it_does: A large US consumer and commercial bank.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: A large deposit base; the regulatory asset cap that limited growth was lifted in 2025.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: Credit losses or renewed regulatory problems.

moat.summary: A strong deposit franchise that spent years under regulatory penalty.

industry.summary: Banking changes slowly, but results depend on credit cycles and interest rates.

management.summary: Current management has repaired much of the damage from past scandals.

financial_health.ratio_gaps: Not available from the data source: net interest margin, efficiency ratio, CET1 capital ratio, loan-loss reserves and tangible book value. Read them in the 10-K before acting.

valuation.method: Banks are valued on book value, not free cash flow. Justified price-to-book = (ROE − 3% growth) ÷ (required return − 3%), using a normalised ROE of 10.7% (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM, capped at 25%) and a required return of 11% (low) to 9% (high): 0.96–1.28 × book value per share of $58.92.

methods.name: Excess-return model on book value
methods.basis: Book value per share $58.92 × 0.96–1.28. This is how Damodaran values banks and insurers: equity is worth book value plus the returns earned above the cost of equity.
